traveler: Baha ud-Din Walad (Baha' al-Din Muhammad ibn Husayn al-Khatibi, Sultan al-Ulama)
title: The Book Carried West: from the Vakhsh River to the Rose Garden of Konya
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Balkh, the birth of Baha ud-Din Walad
stops.date_confidence: contested: 543 AH / 1148 in Persian Wikipedia; Turkish Wikipedia gives a range, 1148/1152; Encyclopaedia Iranica gives 546-628 AH, i.e. birth 1151. No source fixes a month or day; defaulted to 01-01. Not resolved.
stops.campa: A son is born to the house of al-Khatibi at Balkh, Baha ud-Din Muhammad ibn Husayn, into a line of Hanafi jurists who hold the pulpit and the law court of the city together. The chroniclers who come after will call him Sultan al-Ulama, Sultan of the Scholars, and will set his whole life at Balkh because Balkh is the greater name. The documents will say otherwise. He is born into a Khwarazmian world that has perhaps sixty years left to it, and he will outlive its eastern half by a decade.
suggested_refs: The No Gonbad mosque quarter of Balkh, traditional seat of the al-Khatibi household

stops.name: Balkh, the lineage and the title
stops.date_confidence: no date attached to either claim in any source; 1200 is a placeholder for his mature preaching years at Balkh
stops.campa: The Kubrawi tradition of Transoxiana claims him as a disciple of Najm al-Din Kubra, and later Mevlevi writers will say the Prophet conferred the title Sultan al-Ulama on him in a dream. His own Ma'arif records something smaller: one spiritually elect man dreamt of an illumined elder who addressed him by that name. Franklin Lewis reads the honorific as posthumous, applied backward by his son's followers. Baha ud-Din preaches in Balkh under a name that, in his lifetime, no document gives him.
stops.quote: O Sultan al-Ulama, come out so that the world may be filled with light...
stops.quote_source: Baha' al-Din Walad, Ma'arif, as read by Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West, p. 54
suggested_refs: Franklin Lewis's account of the Sultan al-Ulama title as a retrospective honorific
sources: Ibrahim Gamard, 'Common Misconceptions About Rumi', dar-al-masnavi.org, quoting Lewis p. 54

stops.name: Wakhsh, the pulpit and the waqf
stops.date_confidence: the waqf-nama covers a long stretch of years without fixing one; en-wiki dates his residence there as ending 1212. 1204 is a midpoint, reconstruction
stops.campa: East of Balkh, on the river Vakhsh in the province of Khuttalan, a waqf document names him preacher and jurisconsult of the small town of Wakhsh. The paper is dry and administrative and it is worth more than every miracle story told about him: it fixes the family's actual address for years. Fereydun Nafiz Uzluk finds it; Franklin Lewis builds the modern chronology on it. The town is the place later called Sangtuda, on the east bank, and not the modern town that carries the name Vakhsh thirty-five kilometres away.
suggested_refs: The waqf-nama of Wakhsh, found by Fereydun Nafiz Uzluk, naming Baha ud-Din preacher and jurisconsult
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West (2000)

stops.name: Wakhsh, the birth of Jalal al-Din
stops.date_confidence: attested: en-wiki gives 30 September 1207 for the birth and Wakhsh for the place; the hagiographic tradition places the birth at Balkh instead, and the two accounts cannot both be literally true
stops.campa: In the house at Wakhsh a son is born to Baha ud-Din Walad and his wife, and they name him Jalal al-Din Muhammad. The world will call him Rumi, after a country he has not yet seen and his father has not yet decided to cross into. The hagiographers will move the birth to Balkh, where the family's dignity sits better. His father's post is documented here, at the river, and here the atlas puts the cradle. The mother is named Mu'mina Khatun in one line of the tradition and Gohar Khatun in another.
suggested_refs: Fritz Meier's philological argument for Wakhsh over Balkh as the family's home base
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Wakhsh, the Ma'arif
stops.date_confidence: the Ma'arif is undated and was compiled across decades; 1210 marks it in the Wakhsh years by reconstruction only
stops.campa: He keeps a book that is not a treatise and not a diary: sermons, dream visions, quarrels with God and with himself, set down in Persian prose as they come. He writes of divine beauty manifesting through his own body until his parts turn to a rose garden. Rumi will carry this book west, and quote it from the pulpit at Konya forty years after his father's death. The Ma'arif is the one thing of Baha ud-Din's that survives him intact and unretold by anybody else.
stops.quote: I saw that God had made to appear a hundred thousand fragrant herbs, rose and rose-garden, jasmine yellow and white, and had converted the parts of me into a rose-bower.
stops.quote_source: Baha' al-Din Walad, Kitab al-Ma'arif, ch. 1, tr. attributed to A. J. Arberry, reproduced at dar-al-masnavi.org
suggested_refs: The Kitab al-Ma'arif, Baha ud-Din's own Persian prose notebook
sources: Ibrahim Gamard, 'Selections from Baha'uddin Walad's Book', dar-al-masnavi.org

stops.name: Balkh, against Fakhr al-Din Razi
stops.date_confidence: the polemic in the Ma'arif is undated; the confrontation narrative around it is Aflaki-derived and carries no year. 1208 is reconstruction
stops.campa: From the pulpit he goes after Fakhr al-Din Razi, the greatest theologian of the age and an ornament of the Khwarazmshah's court, for building faith out of philosophical proof rather than out of revealed miracle. The court scholars hear a preacher pulling the sultan's own following away from the sultan's own men. Whether the two ever stood in one room is recorded nowhere outside Aflaki, who wrote a century later and had a story to finish. The sentence in the Ma'arif is Baha ud-Din's own.
stops.quote: taken refuge in two or three dark corners while abandoning the numerous miracles and proofs [of positive religion]
stops.quote_source: Baha' al-Din Walad, Ma'aref, vol. I, p. 82, quoted in Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Baha'-al-Din Mohammad Walad'
suggested_refs: Fakhr al-Din Razi's rationalist theology, the target of the Ma'arif's polemic

stops.name: Balkh, two rulers in one region
stops.date_confidence: legendary; no chancery record. The year is a reconstruction placed just before the traditional departure
stops.campa: Muhammad II Khwarazmshah, so the tradition runs, sends word that two rulers cannot coexist in one region, and Baha ud-Din is to leave Balkh. It is the line every retelling keeps, because it makes the preacher the equal of the shah and the exile a kind of coronation. No chancery record of it exists. Franklin Lewis treats the whole causal story with care and no belief. Within a few years the household is on the road west, and it never comes back to Balkh.
suggested_refs: The Aflaki tradition of the Khwarazmshah's expulsion order
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Balkh, the household takes the western road
stops.date_confidence: contested: fa-wiki gives 609-610 AH, roughly 1212-1214; en-wiki puts the family at Samarkand around 1212; rumi.journey.json narrates the departure as 1219. Not resolved here
stops.campa: He gathers the household, the disciples and the books, and takes the western road. The reason given depends on who is telling it: the Mongols, who will not reach Balkh for another eight years; the shah's displeasure; or, in his grandson's account, plain injury, the people of Balkh having offended him. The family will not settle anywhere for ten years. The road he starts on now runs sixteen years and ends at Konya, and it outlasts the empire he starts it in.
stops.quote: Sultan Valad wrote that his grandfather had migrated because the people of Balkh offended him and broke his heart.
stops.quote_source: w1.semazen.net, 'The Life of Baha al-Din Valad', paraphrasing Sultan Walad's Ibtida-nama; not a verbatim translation of the primary text
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad, Ibtida-nama, the family's own account of the migration
sources: w1.semazen.net, 'The Life of Baha al-Din Valad'

segments.name: Khorasan, and the News from the East

stops.name: Samarkand, the first stage west
stops.date_confidence: attested loosely: en-wiki 'Rumi' and en-wiki 'Sangtuda' both give the move to Samarkand as around 1212, when Rumi was around five. Month is reconstruction
stops.campa: The caravan comes up to Samarkand, the first great city of the road west, with Jalal al-Din about five years old. The family is out of Khuttalan and out of the shah's reach, moving through a Transoxiana that still has its walls, its libraries, its markets, and eight years of life left. Genghis Khan is at this moment a rumour in the far east of the world, a name that means nothing yet to a preacher travelling with children. Nobody in the caravan is calling this an exodus. There is a destination in mind, and a road behind them that still leads home.
suggested_refs: Pre-Mongol Samarkand, the Khwarazmian empire's second city

stops.name: Nishapur, at the door of Attar
stops.date_confidence: inherited from rumi.journey.json and attar.journey.json, which both date the meeting June 1219; no contemporary source fixes any year, and other reconstructions place it as late as the 1220s
stops.campa: At Nishapur the caravan halts and the house of Farid al-Din Attar opens to it. Attar is old, author of the Conference of the Birds, keeper of a poetry of annihilation that Rumi will spend his life answering. In Attar's own journey the scene stands recorded from the other side: a scholar out of Balkh, fleeing west with his household ahead of a horror gathering in the east. Two men who never meet again stand once in the same courtyard, and one of them notices the boy.
suggested_refs: Attar's house at Nishapur, the meeting recorded from both sides in the atlas

stops.name: Nishapur, the Asrar-nama
stops.date_confidence: tradition only; the chronology is contested and some modern scholars doubt the meeting occurred at all. Date inherited from the atlas's own Nishapur stop
stops.campa: Attar puts the Asrar-nama, the Book of Secrets, into the boy's hands and tells the father that this son will one day set fire to the souls of the world's lovers. The scene is in Dawlatshah and in Aflaki and in every Persian retelling since, and in no document contemporary with either man. The Mevlevi order hangs its own lineage on that doorway. Where other orders trace a succession through a chain of masters, this one traces it to a book put into the hands of a child.
suggested_refs: Attar's Asrar-nama, the book given at Nishapur in the tradition

stops.name: Samarkand, the siege in Aflaki's telling
stops.date_confidence: irreconcilable: Aflaki puts the family inside Samarkand during a Mongol siege; genghis_khan.journey.json dates the fall of Samarkand to 16 March 1220, by which time every other account has the household a thousand miles west. Kept, out of geographic order, because the sources keep it
stops.campa: Aflaki sets the family inside Samarkand while the Mongols press the walls, and tells of a terrified woman throwing herself against the boy Jalal al-Din for protection while his father intercedes. By every other reckoning the household is a thousand miles west by then, at Baghdad or on the pilgrim road. The story cannot be fitted to the route and it is not dropped either. It survives because the Mevlevi tradition wants its founder's family standing where the world ended, and the map draws the line back east because the sources do.
suggested_refs: Genghis Khan's siege of Samarkand, March 1220

segments.name: Baghdad and the House of God

stops.name: Baghdad, the caravan at the Abbasid capital
stops.date_confidence: the stop is attested in en-wiki 'Rumi' and fa-wiki; no source consulted fixes a year. Date inherited from rumi.journey.json for consistency across the atlas, and is reconstruction
stops.campa: The caravan reaches Baghdad, seat of the Abbasid caliph, the crossroads the whole Sufi network of this atlas passes through: Hallaj died on the Tigris bank three centuries back, Attar came to venerate the place of that execution, Ibn Arabi stayed twelve days. Baha ud-Din is received with curiosity and declines lodging with the great sheikhs in their khanqahs. He does not stay long. He is a preacher with a household to feed and a pilgrimage in front of him.
stops.quote: We came from God. We again are going to Him. We have no strength except for God.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Baha al-Din Walad at Baghdad, w1.semazen.net, 'The Life of Baha al-Din Valad'; no translator or critical edition given, and untraceable to Aflaki, Sepahsalar or the Ma'arif
suggested_refs: The khanqahs of Abbasid Baghdad, offered and refused

stops.name: Baghdad, Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi
stops.date_confidence: hagiography, uncorroborated; the day is invented to keep the stop in order and carries no authority whatever
stops.campa: The hagiographers put Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi in the room, the caliph's own Sufi, master of the order that carries his name, and have the two men exchange courtesies as equals. Nothing corroborates it. The story places Baha ud-Din inside the highest circle of Baghdad Sufism at the exact moment he is a homeless provincial preacher with a family on carts. That placement, rather than the meeting itself, is what the tellers wanted. He leaves the city southward within days.
suggested_refs: Shihab al-Din Umar al-Suhrawardi, shaykh al-shuyukh of Abbasid Baghdad

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba
stops.date_confidence: the hajj is attested as a stage of the route by en-wiki 'Rumi' and fa-wiki; no source contemporary to the journey fixes a year. Date inherited from rumi.journey.json and is reconstruction
stops.campa: He leads the household to Mecca and around the Kaaba, the black cube at the centre of the map, the one pin this atlas repeats without altering: Attar circled it, Ibn Arabi circled it, Hallaj circled it, and six centuries later Abdelkader will circle it twice. The obligation is discharged. Behind him Khorasan is being taken apart city by city, and the road home has closed while he was walking away from it. A pilgrimage begun as a journey ends as an emigration, and the household turns north instead of east.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Grand Mosque of Mecca, shared pin of the atlas's Sufi journeys

stops.name: Medina, the Prophet's tomb
stops.date_confidence: tradition only, from Sepahsalar's Resaleh; no independent record of the visit, and no year fixed anywhere. Reconstruction
stops.campa: North of Mecca the household stops at the Prophet's mosque and the green tomb, the customary extension of the pilgrimage that almost every pilgrim makes and almost no chronicler bothers to record. Sepahsalar puts them here. Nothing independent does. Baha ud-Din is past seventy by the traditional reckoning, a man who has crossed a continent with his family and is about to cross another, standing at the grave of the man whose law he has spent his life expounding from provincial pulpits.
suggested_refs: The Prophet's Mosque at Medina, customary extension of the hajj

stops.name: Damascus, the household in the Umayyad quarter
stops.date_confidence: Damascus is on en-wiki 'Rumi's route list, which is attested; the detail that the authorities wished to keep him and he declined is Aflaki-derived tradition, and no year is fixed. Date inherited from rumi.journey.json
stops.campa: The family comes up into Ayyubid Damascus and stays a while, and Baha ud-Din preaches in the city. The Mevlevi telling has the local authorities pressing him to remain and Baha ud-Din declining. Later retellings fold Rumi's own student years in Damascus into this same visit, two separate stays pressed into one, and modern scholars pull them apart again. The Umayyad Mosque stands over a road the household walks; Abdelkader will teach beneath the same dome six centuries on.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque quarter of Damascus, station of four journeys in this atlas

stops.name: Damascus, an ocean walking behind a lake
stops.date_confidence: two existing atlas files disagree on this same scene: rumi.journey.json dates it August 1220, ibn_arabi.journey.json dates it 1224. The pin here is ibn_arabi.journey.json's, the date is rumi.journey.json's, so the disagreement stays visible. Lewis regards the anecdote as apocryphal
stops.campa: Ibn Arabi, the Shaykh al-Akbar, watches an old preacher pass in the street with a boy walking behind him and says that an ocean is walking behind a lake. It is the most quoted sentence in the whole Rumi legend and the least documented. Ibn Arabi's own dated movements do not sit comfortably against every version of the family's route, and the Mevlevi tellers who love the line best are the ones furthest from it in time. The boy is thirteen or seventeen, depending on which telling holds the calendar.
stops.quote: Glory be to God, an ocean is walking behind a lake.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Ibn al-'Arabi in later Mevlevi tradition, recorded in Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin
suggested_refs: The Ibn Arabi tradition of the ocean and the lake, in its Mevlevi form
sources: Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West

stops.name: Aleppo, under the citadel
stops.date_confidence: inference only: no named primary source places the family at Aleppo, and no incident is attached. The city is on the map on geographic grounds alone and the date is invented to hold its place in the sequence
stops.campa: The land road from Damascus into Seljuk Anatolia runs under the citadel of Aleppo, and reconstructions of the family's route put them beneath it. No source names a stop there, no incident is attached, no host is remembered. The atlas keeps the pin on geographic grounds alone: a caravan going north from Damascus in these years had few other ways to go. Aleppo is the one stage of this journey attested by nothing but the shape of the ground, and it is marked so rather than dropped.
suggested_refs: The Damascus to Anatolia caravan road beneath the Aleppo citadel
sources: Geographic inference from standard caravan routes; no named primary source

stops.name: Malatya, crossing into Anatolia
stops.date_confidence: the stop is on en-wiki's attested route list; the date is inherited from rumi.journey.json, which puts the crossing January 1221. The chronology lens of the research pool gave 1219 instead. Not resolved
stops.campa: The household crosses into the Sultanate of Rum at Malatya, a frontier city of Ala al-Din Kayqubad I. The great mosque that guidebooks attach to the crossing is not yet standing; it goes up under Kayqubad around 1224, after the family has gone west. In Malatya since 1212 lives Majduddin Ishaq, Ibn Arabi's patron and later his father-in-law. Two Sufi households of the first rank hold the same small Anatolian town in overlapping years, and no source says they met.
suggested_refs: The Ulu Cami of Eski Malatya, dated c. 1224 and destroyed in the earthquake of 6 February 2023

stops.name: Nishapur, the city burns behind them
stops.date_confidence: attested: genghis_khan.journey.json dates Tolui's sack of Nishapur to April 1221, and attar.journey.json has Attar die in it
stops.campa: Tolui's army comes down on Nishapur and takes it apart, and Attar dies in the sack. The house that opened to a fleeing scholar out of Balkh two years earlier is gone, the old poet with it, and the boy who was handed a book in that doorway is now a young man in Anatolia with the whole of Khorasan behind him turned to ash. Baha ud-Din chose to keep moving west, and the choice has become a condition of the world; nothing is left behind him to argue with it.
suggested_refs: The Mongol sack of Nishapur, April 1221, and the death of Attar

stops.name: Erzincan, the madrasa and the refusal
stops.date_confidence: date inherited from rumi.journey.json. The Ismati Khatun patronage was tagged attested in the research pool and is corrected down to tradition here: no Seljuk or Mengujekid record outside Aflaki names her
stops.campa: At Erzincan the Mengujekid court receives them, and Malika Ismati Khatun, wife of the ruler, builds Baha ud-Din a madrasa. Aflaki also writes that the party refused to enter Erzincan at all, because of the evil nature of its people, while Jami has them living there four years. Three accounts of one town: hosted, refusing, resident. No independent Seljuk record names Ismati Khatun's patronage, and the reign of Fakhr al-Din Bahramshah, 1162 to 1225, makes the visit possible and no more than possible.
stops.quote: because of the evil nature of its people
stops.quote_source: Aflaki, Manaqeb al-'arefin, vol. I, p. 22 (ed. T. Yazici, Ankara, 1959), quoted in Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Baha'-al-Din Mohammad Walad'
suggested_refs: The Mengujekid court of Erzincan under Fakhr al-Din Bahramshah

stops.name: Sivas, the great mosque
stops.date_confidence: the stop is on en-wiki's attested route list; no source dates the passage, and the year is reconstruction, placed between Erzincan and Larende
stops.campa: Sivas is a major Seljuk city on the westward road, and the caravan passes through it. Its great mosque was raised under Qutbuddin Malik Shah in 1196 and its minaret added around 1213, so the building the family walks past is a generation old and the tower on it barely a decade. Nothing happens here that anyone recorded. The stop exists in the atlas because the route exists, and because a household of forty people moving with carts does not skip a walled city with water in it.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Sivas, built 1196-1197, minaret added c. 1213

stops.name: Kayseri, the blank in the record
stops.date_confidence: route list only; no source dates or describes the stop. Reconstruction
stops.campa: Kayseri between Sivas and Nigde, another walled Seljuk city, another night or another week. The route lists name it and the route lists are all there is. No patron, no madrasa, no dispute, no miracle: the tradition that gave Baha ud-Din a confrontation with the shah of Khwarazm and a blessing from Attar gives him nothing at all in Kayseri. The blank stays on the map, where it shows how thin the record runs once the story has no reason left to embellish it.
suggested_refs: The Seljuk citadel and city of Kayseri on the Sivas to Nigde road

stops.name: Nigde, the mosque going up
stops.date_confidence: route list only; no source dates the stop. The Alaeddin Mosque is dated 1223 in standard Seljuk architectural surveys, so the family may have passed before the masons began
stops.campa: Nigde, where the Alaeddin Mosque is going up under the local Seljuk governor in these very years. The family passes through while the masons work, or shortly before they start; the surveys date the building to 1223 and nobody dates the passage at all. This is the last named stage before Larende, and the road from here runs southwest into the plain where the household will finally stop moving. By now the westward road has run nine years, and the preacher who left Balkh with a following has reached the edge of the country that will keep him.
suggested_refs: The Alaeddin Mosque of Nigde, dated 1223
sources: standard Seljuk architectural surveys for the mosque date

stops.name: Aksehir, the stop that may not have happened
stops.date_confidence: disputed: some secondary reconstructions insert a stop or short residence at Aksehir, while en-wiki 'Rumi' routes the family straight from Nigde to Larende. The weaker of the two traditions, kept and marked
stops.campa: Some reconstructions put a stop or a short residence at Aksehir before Larende; others run the family straight from Nigde and leave Aksehir out of the story altogether. The two route traditions have never been reconciled, and the Aksehir version is the weaker of them. The town lies well north and west of the direct line, which is the difficulty. The atlas keeps the pin and marks it disputed, because an omitted stage is as much a claim as an added one and neither version can be checked against a document.
suggested_refs: The variant Aksehir route tradition in secondary Rumi biographies
sources: Variant route traditions in secondary Rumi biographies

stops.name: Larende, arrival and the madrasa
stops.date_confidence: attested: en-wiki 'Karaman' states that in 1222 Bahaeddin Veled arrived in town with his family and a madrasah was built for them. The research pool's chronology lens gave 1221 and contradicted its own geography lens; corrected to 1222. Month inherited from rumi.journey.json
stops.campa: At Larende, the town the Turks call Karaman, the local ruler builds Baha ud-Din a madrasa and seats him as a resident scholar. After ten years of roads the household unpacks. They will stay seven years, longer than anywhere since Wakhsh, and here the family becomes Anatolian: a marriage, a death, a birth, a grave. The preacher who was ordered out of Balkh for rivalling a sultan is handed a school by a smaller ruler who wants exactly the rivalry Balkh could not tolerate.
suggested_refs: The madrasah built at Larende to house Baha ud-Din Walad's household, 1222

stops.name: Larende, the death of Mu'mina Khatun
stops.date_confidence: attested: en-wiki 'Karaman' states plainly that Rumi's mother died in 1224. The research pool framed the year as disputed, which overstates the disagreement in the sources actually consulted. Month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Rumi's mother dies at Larende and is buried on the ground of the madrasa where the family lives. The mosque that stands over her now, the Aktekke, called Mader-i Mevlana, Mother of Mevlana, is not built until 1370, a hundred and forty-six years later, by Alaeddin Ali Bey to replace the original school. She is buried at a school and remembered at a mosque that did not exist in her lifetime. Baha ud-Din loses in Anatolia the wife he brought out of Khuttalan.
suggested_refs: The Aktekke Mosque (Mader-i Mevlana Camii) at Karaman, built 1370 over the madrasah site

stops.name: Larende, the marriage of Jalal al-Din
stops.date_confidence: traditional, c. 1225; en-wiki 'Karaman' and the Ibtida-nama place the marriage in the Larende years without fixing a month
stops.campa: Jalal al-Din marries Gowhar Khatun, daughter of a local notable, in Larende, with his father still at the head of the household. The son who was carried out of Wakhsh at five is a married man of eighteen in a Seljuk town, and the family's line is rooted in Anatolian soil three years before it reaches the capital. Baha ud-Din arranges what a father arranges. The exile has become a settlement without anyone announcing it, and nothing in the record says he intended to stay.
suggested_refs: The marriage of Jalal al-Din to Gowhar Khatun at Larende

stops.name: Larende, the birth of Sultan Walad
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Persian and Turkish tradition gives 623 AH / 1226 and names Larende; en-wiki 'Sultan Walad' gives 1227 in both lead and infobox and names no birthplace at all. The birthplace is tradition, not attestation, and the divergence is not resolved
stops.campa: A grandson is born at Larende and given his grandfather's name: Sultan Walad, the boy who will one day write the family's own chronicle and found the order that carries all three of them. Baha ud-Din lives to see him. The Persian and Turkish tradition dates the birth to 623 AH and names Larende; the English reference literature gives 1227 and names no birthplace whatever. The child will outlive his father by nearly forty years and his grandfather by eighty.
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad's Ibtida-nama, the family chronicle written by this grandson

stops.name: Larende, the family graves
stops.date_confidence: undated: en-wiki 'Karaman' says other family members were buried at the site without naming or counting them, and no source gives a year. Reconstruction, placed in the late Larende years
stops.campa: Others of the household are buried beside Rumi's mother on the Larende ground, and the sources that mention them do not agree on who or how many. A brother of Rumi is named in one account. No complete list survives. The seven Larende years cost the family more than the ten years of road did, and the graves are the only accounting of it. When the household leaves for Konya it leaves its dead behind in a town it will never govern from, and the Aktekke's later builders keep the site because the graves are already in it.
suggested_refs: The family burial ground at Karaman beneath the later Aktekke Mosque

stops.name: Konya, the sultan's invitation
stops.date_confidence: the invitation narrative is standard in Mevlevi sources and corroborated by none outside them; no source dates it, and 1228 places it shortly before the attested arrival
stops.campa: Ala al-Din Kayqubad I, sultan of Rum, sends to Larende for the old preacher and offers him the capital. Kayqubad is the greatest builder the Seljuks of Anatolia produce, and he collects scholars the way he collects caravanserais. The invitation narrative is standard in every Mevlevi source and corroborated by none outside them. Baha ud-Din, past seventy-five by any reckoning, accepts a last move. The same sultan will rout an Ayyubid coalition near Kharput six years later, in al-Kamil's journey, not in this one.
suggested_refs: The building programme of Ala al-Din Kayqubad I, patron of the last move

stops.name: Konya, the household settles
stops.date_confidence: three-way divergence: en-wiki 'Rumi' gives 1 May 1228; Persian Wikipedia gives 626 AH, roughly 1229; rumi.journey.json gives May 1229. The most precise attested figure is used and the others are not overwritten
stops.campa: The household enters Konya and stops. The journey that began on the Vakhsh river ends at a Seljuk capital in central Anatolia, some four thousand kilometres of road, and no member of the family will go east again. Kayqubad gives them a madrasa. The city is a construction site of new walls and new mosques, filling with scholars fleeing the same Mongol advance that emptied Khorasan. Baha ud-Din has three years left in it. Rumi will have fifty, and Konya will take his name.
suggested_refs: Seljuk Konya under Kayqubad I, refuge of the scholars of ruined Khorasan

stops.name: Konya, head of the madrasa
stops.date_confidence: attested by en-wiki 'Rumi' as his position at Konya; no source dates the installation, and the month follows the arrival
stops.campa: He is installed as head of a madrasa in Konya and preaches before the sultan's court, the position he held at Balkh and at Wakhsh, restored to him at the end of a decade of roads and larger than either. He is styled Sultan al-Ulama in the city, a title Lewis reads as posthumous and the Konyalis apparently already use. He writes in the Ma'arif of sitting in the mosque in the morning while everyone salutes and bows, and of what he understands God to be doing in that moment.
stops.quote: I was seated in the mosque at morning. Everyone was saluting and bowing. I said, 'God is presenting my spirit to them; He is adorning my spirit and showing it to them adorned.'
stops.quote_source: Baha' al-Din Walad, Kitab al-Ma'arif, ch. 13, tr. attributed to A. J. Arberry, reproduced at dar-al-masnavi.org
suggested_refs: The Konya madrasa of Baha ud-Din Walad, inherited by Rumi in 1231
sources: Ibrahim Gamard, 'Selections from Baha'uddin Walad's Book', dar-al-masnavi.org

stops.name: Konya, the book goes on
stops.date_confidence: the Ma'arif is undated throughout; 1230 marks its Konya phase by reconstruction only
stops.campa: The book goes on in Konya. He sets down sermons and visions in which God answers him in the first person, and the Persian prose stays plain, domestic, physical: fruit, bread, gardens, the body. Rumi is in his twenties, learning his father's trade and reading his father's book. Forty years on, the Masnavi will carry phrases out of the Ma'arif nearly unaltered, and scholars will trace the son's whole vocabulary of divine intimacy back to a manuscript its author never finished and never meant for readers.
stops.quote: I gave thouness to thee for this purpose, that when thou becomes distraught in Me, and thy heart is weary of My nearness, thou mayest gaze upon thyself and become busy with thyself.
stops.quote_source: Baha' al-Din Walad, Kitab al-Ma'arif, ch. 6, tr. attributed to A. J. Arberry, reproduced at dar-al-masnavi.org
suggested_refs: The Ma'arif as the acknowledged source-text behind Rumi's own vocabulary
sources: Ibrahim Gamard, 'Selections from Baha'uddin Walad's Book', dar-al-masnavi.org

stops.name: Konya, the death of Baha ud-Din Walad
stops.date_confidence: four-way divergence: 12 January 1231 (en-wiki 'Mevlana Museum'); 628 AH / 1231 (fa-wiki); 1230 (tr-wiki); February 1231 (rumi.journey.json). Persian Wikipedia additionally flags a much earlier alternative, 618-619 AH. Not resolved
stops.campa: Baha ud-Din Walad dies at Konya, three years after the family finally stopped moving. He is past eighty by the earliest reckoning of his birth and past seventy-five by the latest. The road that began at Balkh, or at Wakhsh, and ran through Samarkand, Nishapur, Baghdad, Mecca, Damascus and six Anatolian towns ends in a Seljuk capital he reached only at the end of it. He has been in Konya less time than he spent at Larende, and it is Konya the world remembers him from.
suggested_refs: The dating disagreement over Baha ud-Din's death across the Persian and Turkish traditions

stops.name: Konya, the rose garden
stops.date_confidence: the rose-garden grant and burial are attested by en-wiki 'Mevlana Museum'; the sultan's week of alms is Aflaki-derived tradition. The day after the death is reconstruction
stops.campa: Kayqubad gives over a rose garden as burial ground and Baha ud-Din is laid in it. The tradition adds that the sultan mourned him deeply and distributed alms for a week; Aflaki is the only witness for that. The garden is the seed of everything that follows: his son buried beside him forty-two years later, the dome raised over both, the order grown around the two graves, the Ottoman sultans sending brocade. A preacher told that two rulers cannot coexist in one region is buried by a ruler in a ruler's garden.
suggested_refs: The Seljuk rose garden at Konya, given by Kayqubad I as burial ground

stops.name: Konya, Rumi takes his father's chair
stops.date_confidence: attested by en-wiki 'Rumi' that Rumi inherited the position on his father's death; no source dates the succession, and the month is reconstruction
stops.campa: Jalal al-Din, twenty-four, takes his father's chair at the madrasa and his father's congregation. He inherits a post, a title used of his father in Konya, and one manuscript. He is a jurist and a preacher like his father before him, competent and unremarkable, and he will remain so for fourteen more years. Shams of Tabriz has not arrived. Everything the world means by the name Rumi is still ahead, and the man who brought him to this city to be a jurist does not live to see it undone.
suggested_refs: Rumi's fourteen years as a conventional Konya jurist before the arrival of Shams

stops.name: Konya, Rumi laid beside him and the dome raised
stops.date_confidence: attested: Rumi dies 17 December 1273 and is buried beside his father; the mausoleum is completed in 1274 under the architect Badr al-Din Tabrizi. The grave-opening legend is unverified and could not be traced to any text this session
stops.campa: Rumi dies at Konya in December 1273 and is laid beside his father in the rose garden. Sultan Walad has the mausoleum raised over both graves, the architect Badr al-Din Tabrizi finishing it in 1274, and the turquoise dome goes up that the whole Persian-speaking world will learn to recognise. Mevlevi legend adds that at the funeral the father's grave opened, or the father's body rose to greet the new coffin. The order is founded on the pair of them, and it is founded here.
suggested_refs: The turquoise dome of Konya, completed 1274 by Badr al-Din Tabrizi

stops.name: Konya, the brocade of Abdul Hamid II
stops.date_confidence: attested: en-wiki 'Mevlana Museum' dates the gift to 1894 and attributes the brocade to Mevlana's sarcophagus, not his father's. Month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Sultan Abdul Hamid II sends a gold-embroidered Koranic brocade to Konya and it is laid over Mevlana's sarcophagus. Six and a half centuries after a Khwarazmian preacher was buried in a Seljuk garden, an Ottoman sultan in Istanbul is still paying for the cloth on the grave beside him. The shrine has been enlarged in every century since Tabrizi finished it, the last works running to 1854. Baha ud-Din's own tomb stands in the same chamber and receives no brocade of its own.
suggested_refs: The 1894 brocade of Abdul Hamid II over Rumi's sarcophagus

stops.name: Konya, the shrine becomes a museum
stops.date_confidence: attested: the 1926 decree closed the lodges, the museum opened 2 March 1927, and the name Mevlana Museum was formalised in 1954
stops.campa: A decree of the new Turkish Republic closes the lodges and converts the shrine complex; the doors reopen on the second of March 1927 as a museum, and the name Mevlana Museum is made official in 1954. The dervishes are dispersed and the tombs stay. Baha ud-Din Walad, jurist of Wakhsh, becomes an exhibit in a building he did not live to see. The Ibtida-nama of Sultan Walad, written in this city in the 1290s, is still the primary document behind everything the museum's labels say about him.
suggested_refs: Sultan Walad's Ibtida-nama, primary source for both biographies in the shrine

stops.name: Tehran, the two books called Ma'arif
stops.date_confidence: attested: Nadjib Mayil-i Hirawi's edition, Tehran 1367/1988 (Mowla). Month unknown, defaulted. The research pool left the attribution unresolved; it resolves in favour of Sultan Walad, not his grandfather
stops.campa: A scholarly Persian edition of the Ma'arif-i Waladi is published at Tehran in 1988, edited by Nadjib Mayil-i Hirawi. The book is Sultan Walad's, fifty-six sermons and lectures by the grandson, and it carries a title one word away from the grandfather's. Secondary literature has conflated the two for a century. Baha ud-Din's own Ma'arif is the book Rumi carried; the Ma'arif-i Waladi is the book his grandson wrote after it, and the confusion measures how thoroughly the father was absorbed into the son's house.
suggested_refs: Nadjib Mayil-i Hirawi, ed., Ma'arif, Tehran 1367/1988 (Mowla), the grandson's book, not the grandfather's

stops.name: San Francisco, The Drowned Book
stops.date_confidence: attested by Open Library: HarperSanFrancisco 2003 and 2004, HarperOne / HarperCollins 2005, 2008, 2009. The 2004 HarperSanFrancisco printing is the canonical first trade edition; 2003 is an advance or e-book record
stops.campa: Coleman Barks and John Moyne bring the Ma'arif into English as The Drowned Book: Ecstatic and Earthly Reflections of Bahauddin, the Father of Rumi, published by HarperSanFrancisco and reissued by HarperOne. It is the first time the father reaches an English-language general readership at all, and he reaches it named as somebody's father, in the subtitle, on a list of books sold on the strength of the son. The prose inside is eight hundred years old and reads like a private notebook.
stops.quote: When I utter on my tongue the remembrance of God, it is as though I am bearing fruit.
stops.quote_source: Baha' al-Din Walad, Kitab al-Ma'arif, ch. 6, tr. attributed to A. J. Arberry, reproduced at dar-al-masnavi.org
suggested_refs: Coleman Barks and John Moyne, The Drowned Book (HarperSanFrancisco, 2004)

stops.name: Konya, the article that does not exist
stops.date_confidence: observed 2026; the absence was checked directly against the English Wikipedia search interface, which flags it and invites article creation
stops.campa: English Wikipedia has no article on Baha ud-Din Walad. He appears inside the articles on Rumi, on Sultan Walad, on the Mevlana Museum, on the Seljuk dynasty, and the search interface returns the absence and invites someone to write one. His son has an article in dozens of languages. The preacher who was ordered out of Balkh for drawing away a sultan's following, and who wrote the book his son quoted for fifty years, survives in the reference literature as a paragraph inside other men's entries.
